nameStory: The bruised nassa gets its name from the dark, purplish-brown markings that streak across its shell, resembling the mottled colors of a fresh bruise. The word 'nassa' comes from Latin meaning 'wicker basket,' referring to the spiral ridged pattern that many shells in this family display.
description: The bruised nassa is a small sea snail that crawls along muddy and sandy bottoms in coastal waters. Its spiral shell is typically brown to grayish with distinctive darker streaks and bands that give it that 'bruised' appearance. These marine snails are scavengers, using their keen sense of smell to locate dead fish and other organic matter on the seafloor. They're part of the mud snail family, also known as dog whelks.

idTips.label: Shell coloration
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic dark purple-brown streaks and bands against a lighter brown or gray background that create the 'bruised' pattern

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Cone-shaped spiral shell that feels solid and heavy for its size, with a pointed spire and rounded body whorl

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Surface feels relatively smooth with fine spiral ridges you can detect by running your finger along the shell

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Small snails typically measuring less than an inch long, easily fitting in the palm of your hand

idTips.label: Habitat behavior
idTips.description: Found crawling on muddy or sandy bottoms, often partially buried, leaving distinctive slime trails

habitat: Bruised nassas live in shallow coastal waters along sandy and muddy bottoms in bays, estuaries, and protected shorelines throughout New England. They prefer areas with good water circulation where organic debris accumulates, providing plenty of scavenging opportunities. Look for them in tide pools, shallow flats, and areas where seagrass beds meet sandy bottoms.

seasonality.spring: Active feeding resumes as waters warm, making them easier to spot crawling on the bottom. Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most actively scavenging and easiest to observe in shallow waters. This is the best time for snorkeling or wading to see them alive.
seasonality.fall: Continue active feeding in preparation for winter. Shells become more common on beaches as autumn storms increase wave action.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water but still present. Beach-combing often yields the best shell specimens after winter storms.

funFact: Bruised nassas are like underwater bloodhounds - they can detect the smell of a dead fish from over 100 feet away and will race across the seafloor in a feeding frenzy, sometimes arriving at a food source within minutes of its death!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small mud snails, but the distinctive dark streaky 'bruised' coloration sets it apart from the more uniformly colored relatives. Remember: if it looks like someone gave the shell a black eye, you've found your bruised nassa!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dog whelks' in some references, these are true nassas and shouldn't be confused with the larger predatory dog whelks (like the Atlantic dogwinkle) that drill holes in other shells. The bruised nassa is a peaceful scavenger that cleans up the ocean floor.
compareHints: Since the bruised nassa is the only Phrontis species in New England waters, compare it to other nassas in the family. Unlike the more common eastern mud snail which tends to be more uniformly brown, the bruised nassa's distinctive streaky coloration makes it stand out. It's also typically smaller and more delicately built than most other local mud snails.
